idiom_name: presenter or controller as container + stateless partial with explicit locals (or a ViewComponent)
implementation_notes: Rails' rendering model already separates the roles: the controller or a presenter object assembles the data, and a partial is a stateless template that sees only what is passed to it - `render partial: "cart/line", locals: { line: line }`, or a collection render that hands each child its own local. A ViewComponent class (or a plain presenter) takes the container role when a child needs real behaviour or its own tests, and the rule stays the same: the partial must not reach for extra instance variables. The framework's locals mechanism replaces the classic structure; a hand-rolled state object is only justified for non-HTTP rendering such as mailers or generated documents.
code_sketch:
<%# app/views/cart/index.html.erb - container view: assembles what children get %>

Cart

<%= render partial: "cart/lines", locals: { lines: @cart.lines } %> <%# app/views/cart/_lines.html.erb - stateless child: only its locals %>
    <% Array(lines).each do |line| %>
  • <%= line.sku %> x <%= line.quantity %>
    • <% end %>
pitfalls: Partials happily read controller-assigned instance variables, so an incomplete locals call still renders - pass locals explicitly and treat stray instance variables in a partial as a defect, or the child's real inputs stay invisible.
Collection rendering with spacer templates or partial layouts mixes container decisions into child markup; keep layout choices in the container.
Fragment caching keyed on a mutable object or a stale timestamp serves removed values; key the cache on the record's updated_at or version.
